_README: Hard exclusions and cautions for caninisation candidates: molecules or classes with known
species-specific toxicity or pharmacology in dogs or cats.
PROVENANCE: this list is reviewer-supplied from established veterinary pharmacology, NOT from a
systematic source, and it is certainly incomplete. It exists so that a candidate ranking cannot
silently surface a molecule that is known to be dangerous in the target species. Treat an absent
entry as 'not checked', never as 'safe' - the absence of an exclusion here is not evidence of
tolerability, and every shortlisted candidate needs a real target-animal safety review.
A proper version of this file should be rebuilt from FDA CVM target animal safety reviews, the
Plumb's/veterinary formulary literature, and the MDR1 pharmacogenomics literature.
Fields: class or molecule, species affected, effect, action (exclude | caution).

exclusions.effect: MDR1 (ABCB1-1delta) homozygous dogs - Collies, Australian Shepherds, Shelties and related breeds - accumulate macrocyclic lactones in the CNS and develop severe neurotoxicity at doses tolerated by other dogs. Usable, but requires genotype-aware dosing and labelling.
Cats lack sufficient glucuronyl transferase and develop methaemoglobinaemia and hepatotoxicity at low doses; narrow margin in dogs. Not a viable companion-animal analgesic.
Greatly prolonged half-life in cats through deficient glucuronidation; toxic accumulation on repeat dosing.

Human NSAIDs have markedly narrower gastrointestinal and renal safety margins in dogs and cats than in people; several are contraindicated outright. Veterinary-specific NSAIDs exist, so this space is largely claimed and the bar for a new entrant is tolerability, not efficacy.
Species differences in sensitivity and first-pass metabolism; used in veterinary practice but with different dosing than humans. Not an exclusion, a dosing-study requirement.
Potent insulin secretagogue in dogs causing hypoglycaemia and hepatic necrosis. Relevant as a formulation excipient, not only as an active.
Cats cannot glucuronidate pyrethroids efficiently; concentrated permethrin causes severe, often fatal neurotoxicity. Dog-only products routinely poison cats in the same household.
Retinal degeneration and blindness in cats at higher doses; cartilage lesions in growing dogs. Dose-capped rather than excluded.
Cats show excitation and hyperthermia at doses routine in dogs; species-specific dosing required.
Severe, frequently fatal neurotoxicity in cats; narrow margin in dogs. A recurring accidental-exposure toxicosis.
Formulation excipients tolerated in humans that cause Heinz-body anaemia (propylene glycol) or toxicity in cats. A caninisation programme must re-examine the excipient package, not only the active.
